source_text: Reuertamur nunc ad resurrectionem, cui et alias quidem proprio uolumine satisfecimus omnibus haereticis resistentes; sed nec hic desumus, propter eos, qui illud opusculum ignorant. quid, ait, facient qui pro mortuis baptizantur, si mortui non resurgunt? uiderit institutio ista: kalendae, si forte, Februariae respondebunt illi pro mortuis petere. noli ergo apostolum nouum statim auctorem aut confirmatorem eius denotare, ut tanto magis sisteret carnis resurrectionem, quanto illi, qui uane pro mortuis baptizarentur, fide resurrectionis hoc facerent. habemus illum alicubi unius baptismi definitorem. igitur et pro (mortuis) tingi pro corporibus') est tingi, — 'mortuum' enim corpus ostendimus — *** quid facient qui pro corporibus baptizantur, si corpora non resurgunt? atque adeo recte hunc gradum figimus, ut et secundam apostolus disceptationem aeque de corpore induxerit: sed dicent quidam: quomodo mortui resurgent? quo autem corpore uenient? defensa etenim resurrectione, quae negabatur, consequens erat de qualitate corporis retractare, quae non uidebatur. sed de ista cum aliis congredi conuenit. Marcion enim in totum carnis resurrectionem non admittens et soli animae salutem repromittens, non qualitatis, sed substantiae facit quaestionem.
pass_a_gloss: Let us return now to the resurrection, to which we have indeed satisfied all heretics resisting with our own volume; but nor are we lacking here, because of those who are ignorant of that little work. What, he says, will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise? Let that institution see to it: the Kalends, perhaps, of February will respond to them to ask for the dead. Do not therefore denote the new apostle as author or confirmer of this, so that he might silence the resurrection of the flesh, inasmuch as those who are baptized in vain for the dead do this because of the faith of the resurrection. We have him somewhere defining one baptism. Therefore, to be baptized also for (the dead) is to be baptized for bodies — for we show the body to be dead — what will those do who are baptized for bodies, if bodies do not rise? And so we fix this step rightly, that the apostle also introduced a second disputation equally about the body: but some will say, how will the dead rise? With what body will they come? For, having defended the resurrection, which was being denied, it was consequent to discuss the quality of the body, which was not seen. But it is fitting to engage with this topic with others. For Marcion, not admitting the resurrection of the flesh at all and promising salvation only to the soul, makes a question not of quality, but of substance.

choices.why: Tertullian is addressing Marcion's view of the apostle

rejected: for the defense of the resurrection

pass_b_english: Let us return now to the resurrection. We have already answered every heretic on this point in a dedicated volume, yet we do not drop the matter here, for the sake of those who have never seen that little work. "What will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise?" (1 Corinthians 15:29). Let that practice answer for itself: perhaps the Kalends of February will speak up for those who ask on behalf of the dead. So do not make the apostle the author or guarantor of this rite, as if he invoked it to prop up the resurrection of the flesh — implying that people baptize for the dead in vain, driven by faith in that resurrection. We have him somewhere defining a single baptism. Therefore, to be baptized for the dead is to be baptized for bodies — for we have shown the body is dead — and so the question stands: what will those do who are baptized for bodies, if bodies do not rise? We plant this step firmly, so that the apostle's second argument also deals equally with the body. Some will ask, "How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?" Once the resurrection — which was being denied — had been defended, it followed naturally to discuss the quality of the body, which was not yet seen. But it is proper to take up that topic with others. For Marcion, who refuses the resurrection of the flesh altogether and promises salvation only to the soul, raises a question not of quality but of substance.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the necessary scripture citation (1 Corinthians 15:29) for the quoted clause 'quid, ait, facient qui pro mortuis baptizantur, si mortui non resurgunt?'. The distinction between quality (qualitatis) and substance (substantiae) is preserved. The translation of 'nouum statim auctorem' as 'the author or guarantor of this rite' in Pass B is a valid interpretive rendering of the context.
